title: Navigation, Presentation & Deep Links
scopeHtml: Scope: NavigationStack, NavigationPath, navigationDestination, TabView, sheets, alerts, deep links, universal links, coordinators.

notes.title: Baseline and the navigation mental model
notes.html:
Baseline for this track. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 as the minimum target, SwiftUI-first with UIKit essentials. We use @Observable, NavigationStack, async/await and Swift Testing. Legacy forms (NavigationView, ObservableObject) appear only in sections labelled "old codebases". Anything new in iOS 18/26 is marked verify.

Android equivalent first. In Android you navigate with Jetpack Navigation (Fragments or Compose NavHost) or the Activity back stack. You call navController.navigate("detail/42"), and the system back button pops. In iOS there is no system back button and no hardware back. Navigation is a stack that you own in your own state, and the user pops with the edge-swipe gesture or the on-screen back chevron.

The core idea. SwiftUI navigation is state-driven. The stack is a value (an array of "where we are"). To push, you append to the array. To pop, you remove from it. The view tree is a pure function of that array, exactly like Compose state drives UI.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct RootView: View {
    @State private var path: [Route] = []

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            Button("Open item 42") { path.append(.detail(id: 42)) }
                .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
                    switch route {
                    case .detail(let id): DetailView(id: id)
                    }
                }
        }
    }
}

enum Route: Hashable {
    case detail(id: Int)
}
@Composable
fun Root() {
    val nav = rememberNavController()
    NavHost(nav, startDestination = "home") {
        composable("home") {
            Button(onClick = { nav.navigate(Detail(id = 42)) }) { Text("Open item 42") }
        }
        composable<Detail> { entry ->
            DetailScreen(entry.toRoute<Detail>().id)
        }
    }
}

@Serializable data class Detail(val id: Int)
Android iOS
NavController NavigationStack + a path value you own
Back stack entries Array elements in path
navigate(route) path.append(value)
popBackStack() path.removeLast() or dismiss()
System back button Edge swipe and nav bar back chevron only
Nav graph (NavHost) navigationDestination(for:) registrations
Type-safe routes (@Serializable) Hashable enum or struct values

Real industry examples. Airbnb, Uber and Spotify all keep a per-tab stack plus a modal layer. Large apps wrap the raw path in a router object so features never touch NavigationPath directly (see the router section).

Analogy. A browser history list. Pushing adds a page, popping removes the last page, and you can rewrite the whole list in one go.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying iOS has a "back stack managed by the system". It does not: the path is your state.
  • Assuming a hardware back button exists. Only the swipe gesture and the bar button do; custom back buttons can break the swipe-back gesture.
  • Confusing NavigationStack (iOS 16+) with the legacy NavigationView.

notes.title: NavigationStack and type-safe destinations
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Compose Navigation you register composable("route") entries in a graph, and routes were strings until type-safe routes arrived. In iOS you register a destination per type with navigationDestination(for:destination:). The type of the pushed value picks the screen. This is type-safe by construction.

How it works. NavigationStack is a container that shows a root view and pushes more views on top. There are two ways to push:

  1. NavigationLink(value: x) { label } pushes a value. The stack looks up a destination registered for type(of: x).
  2. NavigationLink { DestinationView() } label: { ... } pushes a view directly (a "view-based" link, eager and not path-aware in the same way).

Prefer the value-based form. It makes the path serialisable, testable and routable from outside the view.

struct ProductListView: View {
    let products: [Product]

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            List(products) { product in
                NavigationLink(value: product) {
                    ProductRow(product: product)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Products")
            .navigationDestination(for: Product.self) { product in
                ProductDetailView(product: product)
            }
            .navigationDestination(for: Seller.self) { seller in
                SellerView(seller: seller)
            }
        }
    }
}

Where to put navigationDestination. Put it on a view that is inside the stack and always present (the List, not inside a lazy row). The registration is looked up by walking the view hierarchy. Placing it inside a LazyVStack row or inside a conditional branch makes the destination disappear when that row is not realised, and you get the runtime message "A navigationDestination for X was declared earlier on the stack" or the link does nothing.

Legacy form (you will meet this in old codebases). NavigationView { ... } with NavigationLink(destination:). It is deprecated since iOS 16. It had no programmatic path, and the isActive: / tag:selection: binding pattern was fragile. On iPad it silently turned into a split view, which is why NavigationSplitView exists now.

Mechanism notes (senior). Each pushed value is stored in the path; the view for it is rebuilt from the destination closure whenever the stack re-renders. This means the destination closure should be cheap and the value should carry only an ID or a small model, not a big mutable object. The view's own @State survives while it stays on the stack and is destroyed when popped.

Real examples. Apple's own Settings, Mail and Notes follow this push model. Production apps pass id values (Route.detail(id:)) and re-fetch in the destination, because a stale copy of a model in the path will not update.

Analogy. A stack of index cards where each card tells you which template to use to render it.

Common interview traps.

  • Using the view-based NavigationLink(destination:) inside a List of thousands of rows: the destination view may be created eagerly, which wastes work.
  • Registering navigationDestination inside a lazy container so it vanishes on scroll.
  • Registering two destinations for the same type on the same stack: the closest one wins, which causes confusing behaviour.

notes.title: NavigationPath and programmatic routing
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you hold a NavController and call navigate, popBackStack, popUpTo. In iOS the equivalent control is the path binding. You have two choices: a typed array ([Route]) or a type-erased NavigationPath.

Typed array vs NavigationPath.

  • [Route] with one Hashable enum: fully inspectable, easy to test, easy to log, simple to deep link. This is what most teams choose.
  • NavigationPath: a type-erased list that can hold several different Hashable types (an Int, a Product, a Seller). It is Codable when the elements are Codable (use path.codable and NavigationPath(representation)), which helps state restoration. You cannot read the elements back out (no index access); you only get count, append, removeLast(_:).
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@Observable
@MainActor
final class Router {
    var path: [Route] = []

    func push(_ route: Route) { path.append(route) }
    func pop() { _ = path.popLast() }
    func popToRoot() { path.removeAll() }
    func replace(with routes: [Route]) { path = routes }   // deep link entry
}

struct AppView: View {
    @State private var router = Router()

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $router.path) {
            HomeView()
                .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
                    route.destination
                }
        }
        .environment(router)
    }
}
class Router {
    private val _stack = MutableStateFlow<List<Route>>(emptyList())
    val stack = _stack.asStateFlow()

    fun push(r: Route) { _stack.update { it + r } }
    fun pop() { _stack.update { it.dropLast(1) } }
    fun popToRoot() { _stack.value = emptyList() }
    fun replace(routes: List<Route>) { _stack.value = routes }
}
// In Compose you still bridge this to NavController or use Navigation 3 (verify)

Programmatic patterns you must know.

  • Pop to root: path.removeAll() (typed) or path = NavigationPath().
  • Pop to a specific screen: path.removeLast(path.count - n).
  • Replace the stack for a deep link: assign a whole new array in one step, which avoids the intermediate animations.
  • Dismiss from a child: @Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss then dismiss(). This works for both pushed views and sheets.

Pitfalls. Mutating the path more than once in the same run loop with animations can produce a glitchy transition on iOS 16. On iOS 17+ it is much better but still test it. If you push after a sheet dismissal, wait for the sheet to finish or you may get "Attempt to present while a presentation is in progress" in UIKit-backed logs.

Real examples. Apps with a custom router (many fintech apps, and open-source projects using FlowStacks or Point-Free's swift-navigation) make the whole navigation state a value type so they can snapshot and replay it in tests.

Analogy. A train timetable you can edit as a whole: delete the last stop, append one, or hand the train a brand new list of stops.

Common interview traps.

  • Trying to read an element out of NavigationPath by index. You cannot; use a typed array if you need inspection.
  • Forgetting Hashable conformance on route types (the compiler error mentions navigationDestination generics).
  • Putting reference types (view models) in the path: they are not Hashable by value, and equality becomes identity-based and surprising.

notes.title: Sheets, full screen covers and popovers
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android a modal is a ModalBottomSheet, a Dialog, a DialogFragment or a new Activity with a dialog theme. In iOS, modals are first-class presentations that sit outside the navigation stack, each with its own lifecycle and its own nested stack if needed.

The three presentation modifiers.

struct FeedView: View {
    @State private var showCompose = false
    @State private var selectedPost: Post?
    @State private var showOnboarding = false

    var body: some View {
        List { /* ... */ }
            // boolean driven
            .sheet(isPresented: $showCompose) {
                ComposeView()
            }
            // item driven: sheet shows when non-nil, dismisses when set to nil
            .sheet(item: $selectedPost) { post in
                PostEditorView(post: post)
            }
            // covers the whole screen, no swipe-to-dismiss
            .fullScreenCover(isPresented: $showOnboarding) {
                OnboardingView()
            }
    }
}

Prefer sheet(item:). With isPresented plus a separate optional you can desync (sheet shown but the item is nil). The item: form makes the content a function of the value, like a Compose if (item != null) branch.

Sheet details.

  • presentationDetents([.medium, .large]) gives a bottom-sheet that resizes. iOS 16+. Custom heights: .height(300) or .fraction(0.4).
  • presentationDragIndicator(.visible).
  • interactiveDismissDisabled(true) blocks swipe-down (for unsaved-changes flows). Pair it with a confirmation dialog.
  • On iPad, sheets are centered cards; on iPhone they are bottom sheets and stack with the "card" look under them.
  • fullScreenCover is unavailable on macOS; it is iOS/tvOS/watchOS (verify per platform).

Popovers. popover(isPresented:attachmentAnchor:arrowEdge:content:). On iPad and Mac it is a real popover with an arrow. On iPhone it adapts to a sheet by default (iOS 16.4+ lets you opt in to a compact popover via presentationCompactAdaptation(.popover), verify).

Dismissal. Inside the presented view use @Environment(\.dismiss). Do not toggle the parent's boolean from the child by passing a binding unless you need to.

Nested navigation inside a sheet. A sheet does not inherit the presenting stack. If the sheet needs push navigation, give it its own NavigationStack.

.sheet(isPresented: $showCompose) {
    NavigationStack {
        ComposeView()
            .navigationTitle("New post")
            .toolbar {
                ToolbarItem(placement: .cancellationAction) { Button("Cancel") { showCompose = false } }
            }
    }
}

Real examples. Instagram's create flow, Apple Maps' draggable detents sheet and Apple Music's Now Playing all use sheet-style modals with detents. Apple Maps keeps a sheet permanently shown using presentationBackgroundInteraction(.enabled) so the map behind stays interactive.

Analogy. A sheet is a sticky note laid on top of the desk; it does not rearrange the folders (the stack) underneath.

Common interview traps.

  • Presenting two sheets from one view with two booleans: only one .sheet per view node is reliable. Use an enum item or attach to different views.
  • Trying to present a sheet while another is dismissing.
  • Expecting a DialogFragment-style result callback. In SwiftUI you pass a closure or write to shared state.

notes.title: Alerts, confirmation dialogs and system prompts
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you show AlertDialog or BasicAlertDialog, and bottom action lists are custom. In iOS there are three distinct native components with clear intent.

Component Use Android analogue
alert Short message, 1 to 2 buttons, centered AlertDialog
confirmationDialog Choose among actions (action sheet) Bottom sheet menu
Menu / contextMenu Inline contextual actions Overflow menu / long-press menu
Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct DeleteExample: View {
    @State private var showConfirm = false
    @State private var errorMessage: String?

    var body: some View {
        Button("Delete", role: .destructive) { showConfirm = true }
            .confirmationDialog("Delete this note?", isPresented: $showConfirm, titleVisibility: .visible) {
                Button("Delete", role: .destructive) { delete() }
                Button("Cancel", role: .cancel) { }
            } message: {
                Text("This cannot be undone.")
            }
            .alert("Could not delete", isPresented: .constant(errorMessage != nil)) {
                Button("OK") { errorMessage = nil }
            } message: {
                Text(errorMessage ?? "")
            }
    }
    func delete() { /* ... */ }
}
@Composable
fun DeleteExample(onDelete: () -> Unit) {
    var showConfirm by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
    Button(onClick = { showConfirm = true }) { Text("Delete") }
    if (showConfirm) {
        AlertDialog(
            onDismissRequest = { showConfirm = false },
            title = { Text("Delete this note?") },
            text = { Text("This cannot be undone.") },
            confirmButton = { TextButton(onClick = { onDelete(); showConfirm = false }) { Text("Delete") } },
            dismissButton = { TextButton(onClick = { showConfirm = false }) { Text("Cancel") } }
        )
    }
}

Rules from the Human Interface Guidelines.

  • Mark destructive actions with role: .destructive (red). Mark the safe exit role: .cancel; the system places it correctly.
  • Alerts are for important, blocking information. Do not use them for success toasts. iOS has no built-in Snackbar or Toast; apps build their own overlay (or use libraries like Toast-SwiftUI, PopupView, verify).
  • Alerts can contain a TextField on iOS 16+ for simple input (verify availability), but a sheet is better for forms.

Presenting from state. Alerts bound to an optional error are common: .alert(item:) was deprecated in favour of alert(_:isPresented:presenting:actions:message:). Use the presenting: overload so the message can use the data.

System prompts are not alerts you build. Permission prompts (location, notifications, camera) are shown by the system when you call the API. You cannot restyle them. You supply the reason string in Info.plist (NSCameraUsageDescription). A missing key causes a crash at the permission request, and App Review rejects vague reasons. Plan a pre-permission "primer" screen because you only get one system prompt per permission.

Real examples. Messages and Mail use confirmation dialogs for destructive swipe actions. Banking apps use interactiveDismissDisabled plus a confirmation dialog on unsaved forms.

Analogy. An alert is a tap on the shoulder; a confirmation dialog is a waiter asking "which of these would you like?"

Common interview traps.

  • Using an alert for a list of choices (it supports only a few buttons); that is a confirmation dialog.
  • Forgetting role: .cancel, which makes the cancel button lose the standard position and tap-outside behaviour.
  • Expecting to customise the iOS permission dialog text beyond the Info.plist string.

notes.title: TabView and per-tab navigation stacks
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you use NavigationBar with a NavHost and saveState/restoreState options so each bottom tab keeps its own back stack. In iOS, TabView is the container, and each tab owns its own NavigationStack. Tabs keep their state automatically while they exist in the view tree.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
enum AppTab: Hashable { case home, search, profile }

struct MainTabs: View {
    @State private var selection: AppTab = .home
    @State private var homePath: [Route] = []
    @State private var searchPath: [Route] = []

    var body: some View {
        TabView(selection: $selection) {
            Tab("Home", systemImage: "house", value: AppTab.home) {
                NavigationStack(path: $homePath) { HomeView() }
            }
            Tab("Search", systemImage: "magnifyingglass", value: AppTab.search) {
                NavigationStack(path: $searchPath) { SearchView() }
            }
            Tab("Profile", systemImage: "person", value: AppTab.profile) {
                NavigationStack { ProfileView() }
            }
        }
    }
}
@Composable
fun MainTabs() {
    val nav = rememberNavController()
    Scaffold(bottomBar = {
        NavigationBar {
            tabs.forEach { tab ->
                NavigationBarItem(
                    selected = /* current destination in tab */ false,
                    onClick = {
                        nav.navigate(tab.route) {
                            popUpTo(nav.graph.findStartDestination().id) { saveState = true }
                            launchSingleTop = true
                            restoreState = true
                        }
                    },
                    icon = { Icon(tab.icon, null) }, label = { Text(tab.label) }
                )
            }
        }
    }) { /* NavHost */ }
}

API versions (important). The Tab(_:systemImage:value:content:) initialiser is the iOS 18 API (verify exact availability). On iOS 17 you use .tabItem { Label("Home", systemImage: "house") } and .tag(AppTab.home). Since your minimum target may be iOS 17, wrap with @available or use the older form.

Behaviour you must know.

  • Re-tapping the active tab should pop to root or scroll to top. iOS gives no built-in callback; you detect it by wrapping the selection binding with a custom Binding(get:set:) and checking if the new value equals the old one.
  • Tab state lifetime: All tab roots are created but body is evaluated lazily; a tab you have never visited has not loaded. Once visited, its @State and stack persist while the TabView lives.
  • Badges: .badge(3) on the tab item.
  • More than 5 tabs on iPhone collapses into a "More" tab automatically.
  • iPad (iOS 18): the tab bar can appear at the top and morph into a sidebar (.tabViewStyle(.sidebarAdaptable), verify).

Deep link and tab together. A deep link typically sets the tab and the target tab's path in one transaction, so keep the selection and the paths in a single observable object (the Router).

Real examples. Instagram (5 tabs with independent stacks, re-tap scrolls to top), Twitter/X, Spotify and App Store all follow the "one stack per tab" pattern.

Analogy. A filing cabinet with separate drawers; opening a drawer does not close the files in other drawers.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting one NavigationStack around the whole TabView: the nav bar and back stack then span tabs, which is wrong.
  • Believing TabView destroys inactive tabs like a ViewPager with offscreen limits. State persists; heavy onAppear work still repeats each time the tab becomes visible.
  • Mixing .tag types (an Int tag with an enum selection) so selection never matches.

notes.title: Deep links: URL schemes and universal links
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you declare an <intent-filter> with <data android:scheme=...> for custom schemes, and use Android App Links with autoVerify plus assetlinks.json served at /.well-known/. In iOS the equivalents are custom URL schemes (Info.plist) and Universal Links (an entitlement plus apple-app-site-association file).

Aspect Android iOS
Custom scheme <data android:scheme="myapp"> CFBundleURLTypes in Info.plist
Verified web link App Links, assetlinks.json Universal Links, apple-app-site-association (AASA)
Server file path /.well-known/assetlinks.json /.well-known/apple-app-site-association (no extension)
App-side opt-in android:autoVerify="true" Associated Domains entitlement applinks:example.com
Verification System verifies at install System fetches AASA via Apple's CDN (verify caching behaviour)
Entry point onNewIntent / intent.data .onOpenURL / onContinueUserActivity

Custom scheme. Register in Info.plist (xml):

<key>CFBundleURLTypes</key>
<array>
  <dict>
    <key>CFBundleURLSchemes</key>
    <array><string>myapp</string></array>
  </dict>
</array>

Anyone can claim a custom scheme, so it is not verified and can be hijacked. Use it for OAuth redirects, internal tooling and legacy support. Prefer Universal Links for anything user-facing.

Universal Links.

  1. Host the AASA file at https://example.com/.well-known/apple-app-site-association, served over HTTPS with no redirects and application/json.
  2. Add the capability Associated Domains with applinks:example.com in the entitlements.
  3. Handle the incoming URL in the app.
{
  "applinks": {
    "details": [
      {
        "appIDs": ["ABCDE12345.com.example.myapp"],
        "components": [
          { "/": "/product/*", "comment": "product pages" },
          { "/": "/internal/*", "exclude": true }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The appIDs value is TeamID.BundleID. The components format is the modern one; the older paths array still exists in old files (verify).

Handling in SwiftUI.

@main
struct MyApp: App {
    @State private var router = Router()

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            AppView()
                .environment(router)
                .onOpenURL { url in router.handle(url) }                        // custom scheme and universal links
                .onContinueUserActivity(NSUserActivityTypeBrowsingWeb) { activity in
                    if let url = activity.webpageURL { router.handle(url) }   // some universal link paths
                }
        }
    }
}

On iOS 14+ with SwiftUI lifecycle, onOpenURL receives both custom schemes and universal links in most cases. Handling both is defensive.

Parsing into a route. Never scatter URL logic through views. Parse in one pure function that returns [Route], which is trivially unit testable.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
extension Router {
    func handle(_ url: URL) {
        guard let comps = URLComponents(url: url, resolvingAgainstBaseURL: false) else { return }
        let parts = comps.path.split(separator: "/").map(String.init)
        switch parts.first {
        case "product":
            if let id = parts.dropFirst().first.flatMap(Int.init) {
                selectedTab = .home
                homePath = [.detail(id: id)]       // replace stack in one go
            }
        default: break
        }
    }
}
fun handle(uri: Uri) {
    val parts = uri.pathSegments
    when (parts.firstOrNull()) {
        "product" -> parts.getOrNull(1)?.toIntOrNull()?.let { id ->
            selectedTab.value = Tab.Home
            homeStack.value = listOf(Route.Detail(id))
        }
    }
}

Cold start vs warm. If the app is launched by the link, onOpenURL can fire before your auth state or data layer is ready. Queue the pending URL and replay it after login or bootstrap. This is a classic production bug: link works when the app is open but is lost on cold launch.

Testing. From the terminal:

xcrun simctl openurl booted "myapp://product/42"
xcrun simctl openurl booted "https://example.com/product/42"

Universal links typed into Safari's address bar do not trigger the app; tapping them from Notes, Messages or another app does. Safari treats a long-press as "open in browser" preference and remembers it.

Real examples. Airbnb, Uber and Spotify use universal links with a deferred deep link flow (Branch or Firebase Dynamic Links). Firebase Dynamic Links was deprecated and shut down in August 2025 (verify); teams moved to Branch, AppsFlyer OneLink or own AASA handling.

Analogy. A custom scheme is a nickname anyone can shout; a universal link is a notarised address that both the website and the app have signed.

Common interview traps.

  • Serving the AASA file behind a redirect or with a .json extension, so verification fails silently.
  • Forgetting that universal links are verified against the domain and do not fire when the user types them in Safari.
  • Assuming the Android assetlinks.json SHA-256 fingerprint idea carries over. iOS uses Team ID plus Bundle ID, not a certificate hash.
  • Handling a deep link before the user is logged in and losing it.

notes.title: State restoration
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you survive process death with SavedStateHandle, rememberSaveable and onSaveInstanceState. iOS has the same problem: the system can kill a backgrounded app, and the user expects to return where they were. SwiftUI offers two tools.

@SceneStorage. A property wrapper that stores small values per scene, restored when the scene is recreated. Think of it as rememberSaveable with automatic persistence.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct RootTabs: View {
    @SceneStorage("selectedTab") private var selectedTab = "home"
    @SceneStorage("draft") private var draft = ""

    var body: some View {
        TabView(selection: $selectedTab) { /* ... */ }
    }
}
@Composable
fun RootTabs() {
    var selectedTab by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("home") }
    var draft by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf("") }
}

Limits: @SceneStorage supports basic types (Bool, Int, Double, String, URL, Data, and RawRepresentable of those). It is meant for small UI state, not model data. Apple warns that it is not for sensitive data and the system may discard it (verify exact guidance).

Restoring a navigation path. Make the route Codable and store the encoded path as Data.

@Observable
@MainActor
final class Router {
    var path = NavigationPath()

    func save() -> Data? {
        guard let rep = path.codable else { return nil }   // nil if an element is not Codable
        return try? JSONEncoder().encode(rep)
    }

    func restore(from data: Data) {
        guard let rep = try? JSONDecoder().decode(NavigationPath.CodableRepresentation.self, from: data) else { return }
        path = NavigationPath(rep)
    }
}

struct AppView: View {
    @State private var router = Router()
    @SceneStorage("navPath") private var stored: Data?

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $router.path) { HomeView() }
            .onAppear { if let stored { router.restore(from: stored) } }
            .onChange(of: router.path) { router.save().map { stored = $0 } }
    }
}

With a typed [Route] where Route: Codable, you can encode the array directly, which is simpler and easier to migrate.

Design rule. Store where the user was (route plus IDs), not the data itself. Re-fetch content on restore. If the content has been deleted, fall back to root rather than crash.

Legacy form. UIKit state restoration used restorationIdentifier and encodeRestorableState(with:). It is deprecated in favour of NSUserActivity and stateRestorationActivity(for:) per scene (verify). Old codebases may still contain it.

Real examples. Notes and Safari restore exactly the page and scroll position. Most shopping apps restore the tab and last screen only, because restoring checkout state is risky.

Analogy. A bookmark in a book: you save the page number, not a copy of the page.

Common interview traps.

  • Saving whole models into @SceneStorage.
  • Not handling a restored path that references deleted items.
  • Confusing @SceneStorage (per scene, restoration) with @AppStorage (UserDefaults, app-wide settings).

notes.title: Router and coordinator patterns
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android teams often wrap NavController behind a Navigator interface that ViewModels or features can call, which is the same idea as a coordinator. In iOS the Coordinator pattern was popularised for UIKit to take navigation logic out of view controllers. In SwiftUI the same idea is a Router (an @Observable object holding paths) and sometimes still called a coordinator.

UIKit coordinator (old codebases). A coordinator owns a UINavigationController and creates view controllers. View controllers talk to it via delegates or closures: "user tapped item", and the coordinator decides what to show next. It fixed "massive view controller" and tight coupling between screens.

@MainActor
protocol Coordinator: AnyObject {
    var navigationController: UINavigationController { get }
    func start()
}

final class ProductCoordinator: Coordinator {
    let navigationController: UINavigationController
    init(nav: UINavigationController) { navigationController = nav }

    func start() {
        let vc = ProductListViewController()
        vc.onSelect = { [weak self] id in self?.showDetail(id) }   // closure, weak to avoid a cycle
        navigationController.pushViewController(vc, animated: false)
    }

    func showDetail(_ id: Int) {
        navigationController.pushViewController(ProductDetailViewController(id: id), animated: true)
    }
}

SwiftUI router. The router holds the path, tab selection and presented sheet. Features receive it via @Environment, or through closures injected by the parent so features do not know about each other.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
enum Route: Hashable { case detail(Int), seller(String) }
enum Sheet: Identifiable, Hashable {
    case compose, filters
    var id: Self { self }
}

@Observable
@MainActor
final class Router {
    var path: [Route] = []
    var sheet: Sheet?
    var selectedTab: AppTab = .home
}

struct ProductRow: View {
    @Environment(Router.self) private var router
    let id: Int
    var body: some View {
        Button("Open") { router.path.append(.detail(id)) }
    }
}
class Router {
    val stack = mutableStateListOf<Route>()
    var sheet by mutableStateOf<Sheet?>(null)
    var selectedTab by mutableStateOf(AppTab.Home)
}

@Composable
fun ProductRow(id: Int, router: Router) {
    Button(onClick = { router.stack.add(Route.Detail(id)) }) { Text("Open") }
}

Trade-offs.

  • A global router is easy and works for most apps. The cost: every feature depends on a shared type, harming modularity.
  • Closure based navigation: each feature exposes onSelect: (Int) -> Void, the parent wires them. Features are reusable and preview friendly.
  • Libraries: Point-Free's swift-navigation and TCA's StackState/StackAction model navigation as state; FlowStacks and SwiftUIRouter-style packages exist (verify current maintenance before adopting).
  • Hybrid UIKit apps keep coordinators and embed SwiftUI via UIHostingController (see the UIKit interop note).

Testing wins. Because routes are plain values, a test can call router.handle(url) and assert router.path == [.detail(42)] with Swift Testing:

import Testing

@MainActor
struct RouterTests {
    @Test func productLinkOpensDetail() {
        let router = Router()
        router.handle(URL(string: "https://example.com/product/42")!)
        #expect(router.path == [.detail(42)])
    }
}

Real examples. Airbnb and Lyft have publicly described coordinator-like routing for UIKit; many 2019 to 2022 era codebases follow coordinators with Combine. Newer SwiftUI-only apps use a router object or TCA.

Analogy. A coordinator is an air traffic controller: planes (screens) never talk to each other, they ask the tower where to go next.

Common interview traps.

  • Passing the router into every view model and mixing business logic with navigation.
  • A coordinator holding a strong reference to a child that holds the coordinator back (retain cycle); use weak.
  • Claiming SwiftUI makes coordinators obsolete. State-driven routing is itself a coordinator, just lighter.

notes.title: Navigation titles, toolbars and the legacy NavigationView
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you place TopAppBar inside a Scaffold per screen and wire actions yourself. In iOS the navigation bar belongs to the stack, and each screen configures it with modifiers.

struct DetailView: View {
    let product: Product
    @State private var isFavorite = false

    var body: some View {
        ScrollView { /* ... */ }
            .navigationTitle(product.name)
            .navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)       // .large is the big collapsing title
            .toolbar {
                ToolbarItem(placement: .primaryAction) {
                    Button { isFavorite.toggle() } label: {
                        Image(systemName: isFavorite ? "heart.fill" : "heart")
                    }
                }
                ToolbarItem(placement: .topBarLeading) { /* custom leading */ }
            }
            .navigationBarBackButtonHidden(false)
    }
}

Key facts.

  • Placement values like .topBarLeading / .topBarTrailing replaced .navigationBarLeading / .navigationBarTrailing in iOS 17 (verify).
  • Large titles collapse as the user scrolls a List or ScrollView. This works only if the scroll view is the first content view.
  • Hiding the back button (navigationBarBackButtonHidden(true)) also disables the swipe-back gesture unless you restore it with UIKit tricks. Avoid it for normal flows.
  • searchable(text:) adds a system search field in the bar, with suggestions and scopes. That replaces a custom Compose SearchBar.
  • .toolbar(.hidden, for: .tabBar) hides the tab bar on a pushed screen.

Legacy NavigationView (you will meet this in old codebases). Deprecated since iOS 16. Typical old code:

NavigationView {
    List(items) { item in
        NavigationLink(destination: DetailView(item: item)) { Text(item.name) }
    }
    .navigationBarTitle("Items")        // deprecated modifier
}
.navigationViewStyle(StackNavigationViewStyle())   // forced single column on iPad

Migration steps: replace with NavigationStack for iPhone-style push navigation or NavigationSplitView for master-detail on iPad and Mac; convert destination-based links into value links; replace navigationBarTitle with navigationTitle; replace isActive bindings with path mutation.

Production incident patterns.

  • Double push: a fast double tap on a NavigationLink pushes the screen twice on iOS 16 era. Debounce the action or disable the button after the first tap.
  • Nav bar flicker on appearance: setting UINavigationBarAppearance globally in init() is the old workaround for background colour; prefer .toolbarBackground(_:for:) and .toolbarColorScheme.
  • "Update NavigationRequestObserver tried to update multiple times per frame": this console warning appears when you modify the path in several places in the same frame. Consolidate into one mutation.
  • Memory: a pushed view model never freed after pop often means the destination closure captured a strong reference in a long-lived router.

Real examples. Apple Mail uses NavigationSplitView-style three-column layout on iPad. Most social apps hide the nav bar on the feed and use custom headers, which is a conscious trade-off against system behaviour (large titles, swipe back, accessibility).

Analogy. The navigation bar is a shared wall sign; every room (screen) edits what the sign says as you walk in.

Common interview traps.

  • Building a custom top bar and then wondering why swipe-back and large titles break.
  • Treating NavigationSplitView as the iPad variant of NavigationStack without understanding the sidebar, content and detail column model.
  • Using deprecated navigationBarItems.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• SwiftUI navigation is state-driven: the stack is a value you own ([Route] or NavigationPath), and push or pop means mutating it. There is no system back button on iOS.
  • Register destinations by type with navigationDestination(for:) on an always-present view, not in lazy rows. Prefer value-based NavigationLink(value:).
  • Use sheet(item:), fullScreenCover and popover for modals, alert for blocking messages and confirmationDialog for action choices. A sheet needs its own NavigationStack for pushes.
  • TabView hosts one NavigationStack per tab. Re-tap-to-root needs a custom binding. The iOS 18 Tab API differs from the iOS 17 .tabItem form (verify).
  • Deep links come as custom schemes (unverified) or Universal Links (AASA file plus Associated Domains, verified by domain, Team ID plus Bundle ID). Parse URLs into routes in one testable function and queue links that arrive before the app is ready.
  • Restoration stores where the user was, via @SceneStorage and a Codable path, never the data itself.
  • A router (@Observable with path, sheet and tab state) is the SwiftUI form of the UIKit coordinator. Keep it value-based, and unit test it with Swift Testing.
  • NavigationView is legacy (deprecated iOS 16): migrate to NavigationStack or NavigationSplitView.
